title: Rafi and the Long Boat
blurb: Five children, one river race and a boat that leaks. Can Rafi's team stop arguing in time?

chapters.title: The Challenge
chapters.text:
Every year in September, the river village of Muara Teduh held a boat race. The whole village came down to the bank, with drums and flags and stalls selling fried bananas. The older boys and girls usually won, and everybody expected it again. Younger children could only stand in the mud and cheer.

This year, though, the headman made a surprising announcement. He stood on the steps of the meeting hall and waited until the crowd went quiet. "Children from eight to ten may enter a team of five," he said. "You must build your own boat."

A laugh went round the crowd. An old fisherman called out that a boat built by children would make a good home for frogs.

Rafi did not laugh. His heart jumped. He was nine, and he had always dreamed of racing. For years he had sat on the jetty, paddling the air with a stick of bamboo.

He quickly gathered his friends under the jackfruit tree behind the school. There was Tiara, who was clever with numbers, strong Anto, tiny but brave Wulan, and Dodi, who could not stop telling jokes.

"None of us has ever built a boat," said Anto.

"My grandfather builds boats," said Wulan. "He says the first one always leaks."

"Then we will call it The Submarine," said Dodi.

Tiara was counting on her fingers. "The race is in twenty-one days," she said.

"We have three weeks," said Rafi. He looked at his four friends and hoped that they would be enough. "Let us show everybody what we can do."

chapters.title: Building the Boat
chapters.text:
The children began on Monday after school. Tiara walked along the bank, measured the river in long steps and drew a plan on a piece of cardboard. "A long, narrow boat moves faster than a wide one," she explained. "Water has less to push against." She wrote numbers everywhere, on the cardboard, on her arm, and once on Dodi's shirt while he was wearing it.

Anto's uncle gave them old planks of wood from a broken fishing boat. They smelled of salt. Anto carried them two at a time on his shoulder, while the others dragged one between them. Wulan, who was the smallest, crawled into tight corners to hammer in the nails. She hit her thumb twice and did not cry. Dodi sang silly songs to keep everyone happy, and when his arm got tired, he sang about his arm.

They worked every afternoon until the evening call to prayer floated over the water. Then they went home with sore hands. People on the path stopped to look, and some of them shook their heads.

One day, Rafi's father stopped too. He looked at the crooked side of the boat for a long time. "Keep your planks tight," he said, and he walked on. Rafi nodded without really listening.

After ten days, the boat was finished. It was a little crooked, but it was long and bright blue. On the side, Rafi painted its name in white letters: The Swift Fish.

They stood back in the red evening light. None of them had ever made anything so big.

"She is beautiful," Wulan whispered.

chapters.title: A Hole in the Plan
chapters.text:
On Saturday, the children carried The Swift Fish down to the river for a test. It took all five of them, and Anto had the heavy end. The water was smooth and green. They climbed in, grabbed their paddles and pushed away from the bank.

For a minute, everything was perfect. The boat slid along with a soft sound. Tiara counted the strokes. Rafi felt the wind on his face, and he was sure this was the best minute of his life.

Then Dodi looked down. "Er, why are my socks wet?" he asked.

"Why are you wearing socks in a boat?" asked Tiara, without turning round.

"That is not the question," said Dodi.

Water was bubbling up through a gap between two planks. Within seconds, it reached their ankles. Wulan tried to block the gap with her foot, but water began to spurt from the next gap along.

"Paddle to the bank!" shouted Rafi. They paddled hard, but the boat grew heavy and slow, as if a hand were holding it from below. It sank in the shallow water with a soft glug.

The five children stood in the river, soaked and silent. Only the blue tip of the boat showed above the water. The old fisherman went past in his canoe. "Good home for frogs," he said, not unkindly, and he paddled on.

Rafi felt his face grow hot. Keep your planks tight, his father had said, and he had hardly listened.

Even Dodi had no joke. The race was only ten days away.

chapters.title: Too Many Plans
chapters.text:
That evening, the children met in Rafi's yard. They had dragged the boat there and turned it upside down on two logs, where it dripped onto the ground. Nobody knew how to fix the leak. Rafi's mother brought them sweet tea, looked at their faces and went back inside without a word.

"We should paint the gaps with thick glue," said Anto. "My uncle uses it for everything."

"Glue will wash off," said Tiara. "We should start again with new wood. I have worked out how much we need."

"New wood costs money, and we only have ten days!" said Rafi. "We should find some tar. That is what real boats use."

Everyone talked at the same time, and their voices grew louder and louder. Mosquitoes came out. The light began to go.

"You never listen to me!" Tiara shouted. She threw the cardboard plan on the ground. "You always think your idea is best!"

"That is not true!" said Rafi, and his face turned red. "And I am the captain!"

"Who said so?" asked Tiara.

Nobody had said so. The whole yard went quiet.

Wulan covered her ears. Dodi sat in a corner and opened his mouth to say something funny, then closed it again. Soon Tiara walked out of the gate without saying goodbye. Rafi went indoors and shut the door behind him, and Anto and Wulan left in silence.

Dodi stayed a moment longer. He picked up the cardboard plan, smoothed it flat and laid it on the upturned boat. Then he went home too.

The team had fallen apart.

chapters.title: The Race
chapters.text:
That night, Rafi could not sleep. He knew that he had not listened to Tiara. In the morning, he found her plan on the upturned boat, smoothed flat. He carried it to her house and said, "I am sorry. Please tell me your idea."

Tiara looked at the plan and smiled. "I am sorry too. We can do all our ideas. We will use the glue and the tar for the gaps, and we will not need new wood. Glue first, to fill them, and then tar on top."

All week, the five friends worked together. They used glue, then tar, and Wulan tested every plank, crawling along the inside with a lamp to look for any light coming through. Rafi's father came by and pressed a plank with his thumb. He nodded. Dodi's jokes came back, one at a time, like frogs after rain. Nobody talked about a captain any more. Rafi would steer, and Tiara would call the beat.

On race day, the whole village lined the bank. The Swift Fish stayed dry.

The big teams paddled fast, but they splashed and tired. The children kept a steady rhythm: one, two, one, two. Halfway along, they passed one boat, and then another. They came second, only a boat's length behind the winners.

As they climbed out, the old fisherman walked slowly around their boat and looked inside. "No frogs," he said, and he took off his hat to them.

"Second place!" cried Dodi. "Who needs a joke? That was already funny!" Everybody laughed.

questions.prompt: Why could Rafi not sleep that night?
options: The mosquitoes kept biting him all night
He knew that he had not listened to Tiara
His father had shouted at him about the boat
He was too excited about the coming race
questions.why: That night, Rafi could not sleep. He knew that he had not listened to Tiara.

questions.prompt: What did Rafi say when he went to Tiara's house?
options: "I am sorry. Please tell me your idea."
"I am the captain. Please give me the plan."
"It is too late. Please tell the others."
"You were wrong. Please use my idea."
questions.why: He said, "I am sorry. Please tell me your idea."

questions.prompt: How did the team fix the leak?
options: With tar first, and then new wood
With new wood, and then paint on top
With paint first, and then more nails
With glue first, and then tar on top
questions.why: Tiara says, "Glue first, to fill them, and then tar on top." They used glue, then tar.

questions.prompt: How did Wulan test the planks?
options: She poured buckets of river water over the planks
She hit each one of the planks hard with a hammer
She crawled inside with a lamp and looked for light coming through
She pushed the boat into the river and waited
questions.why: Wulan tested every plank, crawling along the inside with a lamp to look for any light coming through.

questions.prompt: What does Rafi's father's nod suggest?
options: He wants them to paint the boat again
He thinks the planks are tight now
He is telling Rafi that it is time to go
He has not really looked at the boat
questions.why: He warned Rafi to keep the planks tight. Now he presses a plank with his thumb and nods, so he is satisfied.

questions.prompt: How did the team solve the argument about the captain?
options: Each had a job: Rafi steered, and Tiara called the beat
They held a vote, and Dodi was chosen as the captain
They asked the headman to choose a captain for them
Rafi was captain for the race, and Tiara the day after
questions.why: Nobody talked about a captain any more. Rafi would steer, and Tiara would call the beat.

questions.prompt: What does the old fisherman mean by "No frogs"?
options: The children must look harder to find some frogs
There are no frogs left in the river this year
He was wrong about their boat, and it is a good one
He is sad because he likes frogs and wants to keep some
questions.why: In chapter one he joked that their boat would be a home for frogs. Now he checks, finds none and takes off his hat, which shows respect.

questions.prompt: What is the main message of the story?
options: The winner of a race is always the best team
Good jokes are more useful than good plans
Boats should be built only by grown-ups
Listening to each other helps a team to work well
questions.why: The team fell apart when nobody listened, and it mended the boat and did well once they used each other's ideas.
